OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for allowing the appeal of Ms. XXXX XXXX and substituting my decision that she is a Convention1 refugee. Ms. XXXX is a citizen of Somalia. On December 11, 2019, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied her Convention refugee protection and found that she is not a person in need of protection. She is appealing that decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

[2] Ms. XXXX claims that she left Somalia for Ethiopia with her mother and siblings in 2006, when she was about seven years old, after her father was killed during a period of war. She left Ethiopia in early 2018 with the help of her uncle, after a war broke out between the Somali people who lived in the region of XXXX, and the Oromo people of Ethiopia. She was separated from her family at that time. Her uncle arranged for her to travel to Canada with a man who accompanied her by plane from Somalia to Toronto, and onward by bus to Edmonton, and then left her at a mall. She has not been in contact with her family or her uncle since she was in Ethiopia. She has not been in contact with the man who she came to Canada with since he left her at the mall in Edmonton.

subthemes.text:
[3] The main issue to address is whether the RPD erred in concluding that, although she has established her nationality as Somali, on a balance of probabilities, Ms. XXXX has not established her personal identity. I find the RPD did err. Ms. XXXX has submitted additional documentation to the RAD, which I find to be admissible, and which establishes her personal identity, on a balance of probabilities. I find that Ms. XXXX is a Convention refugee, based on her well-founded fear of persecution as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years away, with no support in Somalia.

[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision. I have accordingly reviewed all the evidence and submissions and listened to the oral recording of
the RPD hearing. These reasons are based on my independent assessment of the evidence. In arriving at my decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.2
SOME NEW EVIDENCE IS ACCEPTED

[5] The RAD is expected to make its decision based only on the record of the proceedings before the RPD.3 The RAD may accept new evidence and submissions in limited circumstances.4 All new evidence and submissions at the RAD must meet the requirements of section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. According to that section, I can only accept evidence that arose after the RPD decision; was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or that Ms. XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision. If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.5 Evidence that is not considered on its face to be credible or trustworthy is inadmissible in any case.6

[6] Ms. XXXX submitted the following new evidence at the RAD:
a. A Somali birth certificate issued in 2020;7
b. A school record for the 2009 academic year from Ethiopia;8
c. An affidavit from a distant relative who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta;9
d. An affidavit of a friend of hers who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta;10
e. An affidavit of a friend of her mother's who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta.11

[7] For the following reasons, I accept the Ethiopian school record (item b) and the affidavit from Ms. XXXX distant relative who now lives in Edmonton (item c) as new evidence at the RAD.

[8] In regard to the birth certificate, the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Somalia explains that birth certificates are rarely issued in Somalia.12 Furthermore, birth certificates that have been issued are stored in paper repositories.13 There is currently no national system of birth registration in Somalia.14 It can be difficult to obtain a birth certificate later in life without identification documents of the parents.15 One way by which birth certificates can be obtained is if two attending witnesses from the person's clan or subclan, with good knowledge of the applicant, request a certificate from a municipal administration.16 The document provided by Ms. XXXX is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020. It is therefore not from a paper repository. It claims to have been issued at the request of "her family."17 However, there are no further details about how the birth certificate was obtained, except for a reference, in Counsel's appeal memorandum submissions, to Ms. XXXX maternal aunt travelling to Mogadishu to get the document.18 There is no letter or affidavit from the aunt describing how she was able to obtain the certificate or verify its authenticity. Without knowledge of the circumstances in which the certificate was obtained, and acknowledging that very few people in Somalia are issued birth certificates; that document fraud is common in Somalia; and that there are no verifiable Somali identity documents,19 I find this document to be untrustworthy, on a balance of probabilities. I therefore do not accept it as new evidence at the RAD.

[9] I find the 2009 (Ethiopian calendar) school record meets the requirements for new evidence at the RAD. Although the document existed at the time of the RPD decision, I find that it was not reasonably available at that time, because Ms. XXXX had not been able to locate the person who provided the document, a neighbour in Ethiopia. The RPD found that the efforts Ms. XXXX made to contact certain people in order to establish her identity, namely through telephone calls and creating a Facebook page, were not sufficient. The RPD found Ms. XXXX ought to have engaged with the Canadian-Somali community to help establish her identity. I disagree with the RPD's assessment of Ms. XXXX efforts. Ms. XXXX testimony, which was straight-forward, consistent and unembellished, was that her family was not technologically savvy and that she only knew about Facebook, not other social media platforms. Contrary to the RPD's findings, Ms. XXXX did approach a Somali association to help her to establish her identity, which association is meaningfully connected with the Canadian-Somali community.

[10] I find Ms. XXXX made reasonable efforts to connect with family and relatives who do not live in Canada or who she was not aware of, given her circumstances as someone who came to Canada alone, with limited or no language or technological skills. She was unable to make connections by the time of the RPD hearing but was able to do so after the hearing. I have commented below regarding people who she knew were living in Canada at the time of the RPD decision. I find the school document was not reasonably available to her at the time of the RPD decision because she had been unable to locate someone in Ethiopia to help her obtain the document at the time of the RPD decision. Furthermore, it is relevant as it corroborates her testimony that she was in Ethiopia prior to coming to Canada, and it is credible on its face. Although I note there is a spelling mistake in the name of the school district, which is indicated as "XXXX XXXX XXXX,"20 that single flaw does not render the document untrustworthy. To find so would be holding the school system in XXXX to inappropriate western standards.

[11] For the same reasons as above regarding Ms. XXXX efforts to locate people to establish her identity, I find the affidavit from Ms. XXXX distant relative, who now lives in Edmonton, was not reasonably available to Ms. XXXX at the RPD. I find Ms. XXXX was not aware that this relative, who last saw her when she was three years old, lived in Canada. Furthermore, the affidavit is relevant, as it speaks directly to her presence in Somalia as a young child; and it is credible on its face as a properly sworn affidavit with attached identification.

[12] I do not accept the remaining two affidavits as new evidence at the RAD. The reason for this is that I find these two documents were reasonably available to Ms. XXXX at the time of the RPD decision. Each of the documents indicates that the affiant knew Ms. XXXX in Ethiopia, and that they returned to Canada after visiting with her in Ethiopia. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that Ms. XXXX knew these two affiants lived in Canada, since they had visited her in Ethiopia while they lived in Canada. However, based on her testimony at the RPD, I find she did not make efforts to locate them for the purpose of verifying her identity once she got to Canada. Unlike the situation with her neighbour in Ethiopia and her distant relative, Ms. XXXX
was aware that these people lived in Canada. I find that it is reasonable to expect her to have made some efforts to locate these affiants. Therefore, these affidavits are not accepted as new evidence at the RAD.

An oral hearing may be held at the RAD where the new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; is central to my decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.21 In this case, I am accepting two documents, including the truth of the contents of the documents: the school record is a third party document and appears to be a bona fide school record; and the affidavit of Mr. XXXX attests to the affiant knowing Ms. XXXX as a small child in Somalia. It is detailed and uncontradicted. Furthermore, nothing in the affidavit or in the circumstances of its creation raises a serious issue with respect to Ms. XXXX credibility. An oral hearing is not required in these circumstances.
MS. XXXX HAS ESTABLISHED HER IDENTITY

[14] Based on the totality of the evidence in front of me, including Ms. XXXX documentary evidence and her credible testimony, I find that she has established both her national and her personal identity, on a balance of probabilities. The RPD found that Ms. XXXX had established her identity as a National of Somalia, through a letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, along with the testimony of the author of that letter. I agree. The RPD found, however, that Ms. XXXX had not established her personal identity. Ms. XXXX has now provided additional documentation, which I have accepted, to establish her personal identity. In particular, the affidavit of Mr. XXXX states that he is a distant relative of Ms. XXXX; that he has known her since she was born; and that he visited with her family in Mogadishu when she was three years old. Together with her other identity evidence including her credible testimony, I find Ms. XXXX has established her personal identity.
MS. XXXX IS A CONVENTION REFUGEE

subthemes.text:
[17] The NDP for Somalia indicates that it is against culture and religion for a Somali woman to live alone.22 Single women without male support are frequently denied justice in Somalia, and must rely on male and clan support for protection.23 Ms. XXXX has not been in Somalia for most of her life. She has no male support in Somalia. Although the NDP explains that women who have lost their fathers may be taken in by their community, this is only true for those women who have not broken any social norms.24 If the community believes a woman has broken such a norm, she will not be protected. It is not clear whether having lived alone in the West would be considered having broken a social norm.

[18] Considering Ms. XXXX does not have a community in Somalia to begin with, that the clan system if male-dominated and Ms XXXX does not have male family support,25 and that Ms. XXXX may be seen as having broken cultural or religious norms during her time in the West, I find there is a serious possibility that Ms. XXXX will not be protected by her clan if she returns to Somalia. Having strong family and clan networks is very important to a woman's survival in Somalia, as clans, not the state, provide social safety nets in Somalia. Non-Government Organizations provide very limited and temporary assistance to women.26 Without a support network, and particularly without male protection, women face "enormous challenges in virtually every aspect of their lives."27

[19] Discrimination against single women with no family or clan support extends to their ability to obtain housing. The NDP explains that women are unable to rent housing alone and will need a male relative to access housing. Forced evictions are common.28 Discrimination against women also extends to employment. Women have limited employment options, and commonly require references and male support, or endorsement from clan elders, to obtain employment. Women face harassment, threats, and verbal, sexual and physical violence, including from their clan members, when they are required to work outside the home.29 Similarly, women must have male guarantors to obtain bank loans.30 Finally, the NDP explains that gender-based violence in Somalia is endemic, and carried out without impunity.31

[20] In evaluating the country information for Somalia, as well as Ms. XXXX credible testimony regarding her personal circumstances, I find that the level of discrimination faced by women in Ms. XXXX position, specifically single women returning to Somalia after several years away, with no family or clan support, rises to the level of persecution. Furthermore, it is well-established that Somalia has experienced armed conflict for three decades and that state protection in Somalia is not adequate.32 Finally, the NDP evidence is that these risks are prevalent throughout Somalia for women in Ms. XXXX circumstance. She therefore does not have an Internal Flight Alternative. I find Ms. XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution, as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years away and without any support, if she is returned to Somalia.

[16] As noted above, Ms. XXXX testimony was straight-forward, consistent and unembellished, and I find her to be a credible witness. Ms. XXXX testified that she has not been to Somalia since she was a young child, and that she has no family network there. She testified, and I accept, that she is not aware of the whereabouts of any of her siblings or her mother. She has a grade XXXX level of education.

[17] The NDP for Somalia indicates that it is against culture and religion for a Somali woman to live alone.22 Single women without male support are frequently denied justice in Somalia, and must rely on male and clan support for protection.23 Ms. XXXX has not been in Somalia for most of her life. She has no male support in Somalia. Although the NDP explains that women who have lost their fathers may be taken in by their community, this is only true for those women who have not broken any social norms.24 If the community believes a woman has broken such a norm, she will not be protected. It is not clear whether having lived alone in the West would be considered having broken a social norm.

[18] Considering Ms. XXXX does not have a community in Somalia to begin with, that the clan system if male-dominated and Ms XXXX does not have male family support,25 and that Ms. XXXX may be seen as having broken cultural or religious norms during her time in the West, I find there is a serious possibility that Ms. XXXX will not be protected by her clan if she returns to Somalia. Having strong family and clan networks is very important to a woman's survival in Somalia, as clans, not the state, provide social safety nets in Somalia. Non-Government Organizations provide very limited and temporary assistance to women.26 Without a support network, and particularly without male protection, women face "enormous challenges in virtually every aspect of their lives."27

[19] Discrimination against single women with no family or clan support extends to their ability to obtain housing. The NDP explains that women are unable to rent housing alone and will need a male relative to access housing. Forced evictions are common.28 Discrimination against women also extends to employment. Women have limited employment options, and commonly require references and male support, or endorsement from clan elders, to obtain employment. Women face harassment, threats, and verbal, sexual and physical violence, including from their clan members, when they are required to work outside the home.29 Similarly, women must have male guarantors to obtain bank loans.30 Finally, the NDP explains that gender-based violence in Somalia is endemic, and carried out without impunity.31

[20] In evaluating the country information for Somalia, as well as Ms. XXXX credible testimony regarding her personal circumstances, I find that the level of discrimination faced by women in Ms. XXXX position, specifically single women returning to Somalia after several years away, with no family or clan support, rises to the level of persecution. Furthermore, it is well-established that Somalia has experienced armed conflict for three decades and that state protection in Somalia is not adequate.32 Finally, the NDP evidence is that these risks are prevalent throughout Somalia for women in Ms. XXXX circumstance. She therefore does not have an Internal Flight Alternative. I find Ms. XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution, as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years away and without any support, if she is returned to Somalia.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] These are my reasons for allowing the appeal of Ms. XXXX XXXX and substituting my decision that she is a Convention1 refugee. Ms. XXXX is a citizen of Somalia. On December 11, 2019, the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denied her Convention refugee protection and found that she is not a person in need of protection. She is appealing that decision to the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

[2] Ms. XXXX claims that she left Somalia for Ethiopia with her mother and siblings in 2006, when she was about seven years old, after her father was killed during a period of war. She left Ethiopia in early 2018 with the help of her uncle, after a war broke out between the Somali people who lived in the region of XXXX, and the Oromo people of Ethiopia. She was separated from her family at that time. Her uncle arranged for her to travel to Canada with a man who accompanied her by plane from Somalia to Toronto, and onward by bus to Edmonton, and then left her at a mall. She has not been in contact with her family or her uncle since she was in Ethiopia. She has not been in contact with the man who she came to Canada with since he left her at the mall in Edmonton.

[3] The main issue to address is whether the RPD erred in concluding that, although she has established her nationality as Somali, on a balance of probabilities, Ms. XXXX has not established her personal identity. I find the RPD did err. Ms. XXXX has submitted additional documentation to the RAD, which I find to be admissible, and which establishes her personal identity, on a balance of probabilities. I find that Ms. XXXX is a Convention refugee, based on her well-founded fear of persecution as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years away, with no support in Somalia.

[4] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision. I have accordingly reviewed all the evidence and submissions and listened to the oral recording of
the RPD hearing. These reasons are based on my independent assessment of the evidence. In arriving at my decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson Guidelines 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.2
SOME NEW EVIDENCE IS ACCEPTED

[5] The RAD is expected to make its decision based only on the record of the proceedings before the RPD.3 The RAD may accept new evidence and submissions in limited circumstances.4 All new evidence and submissions at the RAD must meet the requirements of section 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. According to that section, I can only accept evidence that arose after the RPD decision; was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or that Ms. XXXX could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before its decision. If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.5 Evidence that is not considered on its face to be credible or trustworthy is inadmissible in any case.6

[6] Ms. XXXX submitted the following new evidence at the RAD:
a. A Somali birth certificate issued in 2020;7
b. A school record for the 2009 academic year from Ethiopia;8
c. An affidavit from a distant relative who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta;9
d. An affidavit of a friend of hers who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta;10
e. An affidavit of a friend of her mother's who was born in Somalia and now lives in Edmonton, Alberta.11
[7] For the following reasons, I accept the Ethiopian school record (item b) and the affidavit from Ms. XXXX distant relative who now lives in Edmonton (item c) as new evidence at the RAD.

[8] In regard to the birth certificate, the National Documentation Package (NDP) for Somalia explains that birth certificates are rarely issued in Somalia.12 Furthermore, birth certificates that have been issued are stored in paper repositories.13 There is currently no national system of birth registration in Somalia.14 It can be difficult to obtain a birth certificate later in life without identification documents of the parents.15 One way by which birth certificates can be obtained is if two attending witnesses from the person's clan or subclan, with good knowledge of the applicant, request a certificate from a municipal administration.16 The document provided by Ms. XXXX is dated XXXX XXXX XXXX/2020. It is therefore not from a paper repository. It claims to have been issued at the request of "her family."17 However, there are no further details about how the birth certificate was obtained, except for a reference, in Counsel's appeal memorandum submissions, to Ms. XXXX maternal aunt travelling to Mogadishu to get the document.18 There is no letter or affidavit from the aunt describing how she was able to obtain the certificate or verify its authenticity. Without knowledge of the circumstances in which the certificate was obtained, and acknowledging that very few people in Somalia are issued birth certificates; that document fraud is common in Somalia; and that there are no verifiable Somali identity documents,19 I find this document to be untrustworthy, on a balance of probabilities. I therefore do not accept it as new evidence at the RAD.

[9] I find the 2009 (Ethiopian calendar) school record meets the requirements for new evidence at the RAD. Although the document existed at the time of the RPD decision, I find that it was not reasonably available at that time, because Ms. XXXX had not been able to locate the person who provided the document, a neighbour in Ethiopia. The RPD found that the efforts Ms. XXXX made to contact certain people in order to establish her identity, namely through telephone calls and creating a Facebook page, were not sufficient. The RPD found Ms. XXXX ought to have engaged with the Canadian-Somali community to help establish her identity. I disagree with the RPD's assessment of Ms. XXXX efforts. Ms. XXXX testimony, which was straight-forward, consistent and unembellished, was that her family was not technologically savvy and that she only knew about Facebook, not other social media platforms. Contrary to the RPD's findings, Ms. XXXX did approach a Somali association to help her to establish her identity, which association is meaningfully connected with the Canadian-Somali community.

[10] I find Ms. XXXX made reasonable efforts to connect with family and relatives who do not live in Canada or who she was not aware of, given her circumstances as someone who came to Canada alone, with limited or no language or technological skills. She was unable to make connections by the time of the RPD hearing but was able to do so after the hearing. I have commented below regarding people who she knew were living in Canada at the time of the RPD decision. I find the school document was not reasonably available to her at the time of the RPD decision because she had been unable to locate someone in Ethiopia to help her obtain the document at the time of the RPD decision. Furthermore, it is relevant as it corroborates her testimony that she was in Ethiopia prior to coming to Canada, and it is credible on its face. Although I note there is a spelling mistake in the name of the school district, which is indicated as "XXXX XXXX XXXX,"20 that single flaw does not render the document untrustworthy. To find so would be holding the school system in XXXX to inappropriate western standards.

[11] For the same reasons as above regarding Ms. XXXX efforts to locate people to establish her identity, I find the affidavit from Ms. XXXX distant relative, who now lives in Edmonton, was not reasonably available to Ms. XXXX at the RPD. I find Ms. XXXX was not aware that this relative, who last saw her when she was three years old, lived in Canada. Furthermore, the affidavit is relevant, as it speaks directly to her presence in Somalia as a young child; and it is credible on its face as a properly sworn affidavit with attached identification.

[12] I do not accept the remaining two affidavits as new evidence at the RAD. The reason for this is that I find these two documents were reasonably available to Ms. XXXX at the time of the RPD decision. Each of the documents indicates that the affiant knew Ms. XXXX in Ethiopia, and that they returned to Canada after visiting with her in Ethiopia. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that Ms. XXXX knew these two affiants lived in Canada, since they had visited her in Ethiopia while they lived in Canada. However, based on her testimony at the RPD, I find she did not make efforts to locate them for the purpose of verifying her identity once she got to Canada. Unlike the situation with her neighbour in Ethiopia and her distant relative, Ms. XXXX
was aware that these people lived in Canada. I find that it is reasonable to expect her to have made some efforts to locate these affiants. Therefore, these affidavits are not accepted as new evidence at the RAD.

[13] I decline to hold a hearing with respect to the two documents which I have accepted. An oral hearing may be held at the RAD where the new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; is central to my decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.21 In this case, I am accepting two documents, including the truth of the contents of the documents: the school record is a third party document and appears to be a bona fide school record; and the affidavit of Mr. XXXX attests to the affiant knowing Ms. XXXX as a small child in Somalia. It is detailed and uncontradicted. Furthermore, nothing in the affidavit or in the circumstances of its creation raises a serious issue with respect to Ms. XXXX credibility. An oral hearing is not required in these circumstances.
MS. XXXX HAS ESTABLISHED HER IDENTITY

[14] Based on the totality of the evidence in front of me, including Ms. XXXX documentary evidence and her credible testimony, I find that she has established both her national and her personal identity, on a balance of probabilities. The RPD found that Ms. XXXX had established her identity as a National of Somalia, through a letter from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, along with the testimony of the author of that letter. I agree. The RPD found, however, that Ms. XXXX had not established her personal identity. Ms. XXXX has now provided additional documentation, which I have accepted, to establish her personal identity. In particular, the affidavit of Mr. XXXX states that he is a distant relative of Ms. XXXX; that he has known her since she was born; and that he visited with her family in Mogadishu when she was three years old. Together with her other identity evidence including her credible testimony, I find Ms. XXXX has established her personal identity.
MS. XXXX IS A CONVENTION REFUGEE

[15] I find Ms. XXXX is a Convention refugee and that her nexus to the Convention is the particular social group of women. Ms. XXXX would be returning to Somalia after several years as a single woman with no family support. The last time she was in Somalia was when she was about seven years old, after her father was killed while he was trying to secure food for the family. Her evidence suggests that she is a member of a majority clan, however I find that as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years with no family support, even as a member of a majority clan, Ms. XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution if she returns to Somalia.

[16] As noted above, Ms. XXXX testimony was straight-forward, consistent and unembellished, and I find her to be a credible witness. Ms. XXXX testified that she has not been to Somalia since she was a young child, and that she has no family network there. She testified, and I accept, that she is not aware of the whereabouts of any of her siblings or her mother. She has a grade XXXX level of education.

[17] The NDP for Somalia indicates that it is against culture and religion for a Somali woman to live alone.22 Single women without male support are frequently denied justice in Somalia, and must rely on male and clan support for protection.23 Ms. XXXX has not been in Somalia for most of her life. It is not clear whether having lived alone in the West would be considered having broken a social norm.

[18] Considering Ms. XXXX does not have a community in Somalia to begin with, that the clan system if male-dominated and Ms XXXX does not have male family support,25 and that Ms. XXXX may be seen as having broken cultural or religious norms during her time in the West, I find there is a serious possibility that Ms. XXXX will not be protected by her clan if she returns to Somalia. Non-Government Organizations provide very limited and temporary assistance to women.26 Without a support network, and particularly without male protection, women face "enormous challenges in virtually every aspect of their lives."27

[19] Discrimination against single women with no family or clan support extends to their ability to obtain housing. The NDP explains that women are unable to rent housing alone and will need a male relative to access housing. Forced evictions are common.28 Discrimination against women also extends to employment. Women have limited employment options, and commonly require references and male support, or endorsement from clan elders, to obtain employment. Women face harassment, threats, and verbal, sexual and physical violence, including from their clan members, when they are required to work outside the home.29 Similarly, women must have male guarantors to obtain bank loans.30 Finally, the NDP explains that gender-based violence in Somalia is endemic, and carried out without impunity.31

[20] In evaluating the country information for Somalia, as well as Ms. XXXX credible testimony regarding her personal circumstances, I find that the level of discrimination faced by women in Ms. XXXX position, specifically single women returning to Somalia after several years away, with no family or clan support, rises to the level of persecution. Furthermore, it is well-established that Somalia has experienced armed conflict for three decades and that state protection in Somalia is not adequate.32 Finally, the NDP evidence is that these risks are prevalent throughout Somalia for women in Ms. XXXX circumstance. She therefore does not have an Internal Flight Alternative. I find Ms. XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution, as a single woman returning to Somalia after several years away and without any support, if she is returned to Somalia.
CONCLUSION

[21] The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that Ms. XXXX XXXX is a Convention refugee.
